messages.subject_clean: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
messages.body_plain:
Hey Marc and all,

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made.

You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.

Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.

In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

Cheers,

John

Subject: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?

Dear all,

I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.

The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.

Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the  recent paper by Goldstein <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14359__;!!Mak6IKo!NX60gBNM93SYmtD8VFgF8ZKITUypQvav83s367dFdyMCCei4DMtHJd5jRIxpf4jgK1znDG6YPKRgyZVRtOJ89-3g$> et al.

My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).

On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.

Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi all,

Marc's question about the definition of a site in camera-trap surveys motivated me to reach out for feedback about an analysis I'm conducting. It's an unusual use case for occupancy modeling, as far as I can tell.

I'm currently working on a data set containing reports of vector-borne diseases in Brazil (dengue, zika and chikungunya). I would like to use spOccupancy to fit multi-season spatially varying coefficient occupancy models to understand the occurrence of these diseases at a national level.

I have daily reports of disease occurrence, including negative test results, per health facility (i.e., 40K sites) for the last 5 years throughout Brazil. For my analysis, I plan to summarize these reports as weekly or biweekly detections. I'm very interested in using the occupancy framework, as these diseases are commonly underdetected and not diagnosed when present. These diseases are present for large periods of time (during summer and fall), so I plan to define seasons as semesters.

Before going forward with my analyses, I would love to hear your thoughts on two particular points:

1. Do you foresee any problem with applying occupancy models to the previously described disease data? Similar to camera traps, people with the disease can go to multiple sites (i.e., attend different health facilities), so the closure assumption might not be reasonable. Marc's email made me think more about the definition of my sites and the need to interpret the occupancy estimates as occurrence.

2. The distribution of the sites (i.e., health facilities) is not uniform. Some health facilities are very close to one another, especially in highly populated areas. If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?

Thanks in advance for any thoughts/recommendations!

Best regards,

Juliana

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

We have written a new stats textbook entitled  Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists – A practical guide to Bayesian and likelihood inference using R, JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan and TMB. The new ASM book provides a gentle introduction to the essential models of applied statistics: linear models, generalized linear models, mixed and hierarchical models. In addition, it introduces integrated models, which have become a mega-trend in statistical ecology during the last 30 years. All models are fit with both a likelihood and a Bayesian approach, using several powerful software packages widely used in research publications: JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan, and TMB. In addition, the foundational method of maximum likelihood is explained in a manner that ecologists can really understand, and every model is also fit by numerical maximization of a custom-written likelihood function in R. Finally, the ASM book contains a comprehensive chapter on model building, checking and selection, all of which topics that are challenging for budding ecological modelers. There is a companion R package ASMbook, which is available on CRAN.

The ASM book is the successor of the widely used  Introduction to WinBUGS for Ecologists (Kéry, Academic Press, 2010). Like its parent, it is extremely effective for both classroom use and self-study, allowing students and researchers alike to quickly learn, understand, and carry out a very wide range of statistical modelling tasks. But in addition, it can be used to learn statistical modeling using a wide range of cutting-edge model-fitting engines, and with Bayesian and likelihood inference alike.

A detailed Table of Contents of the ASM book is attached. For much more information, also about the different target audiences, modes of usage of the book, and tips for instructors and students, please have a look at the book website (here <https://www.elsevier.com/books-and-journals/book-companion/9780443137150>). The website also contains all code for free download, as well as a free bonus chapter on the binomial N-mixture model. That chapter demonstrates the use for model fitting of the R packages unmarked and  ubms, and of the software JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan and TMB, as well as of the “do-it-yourself maximum likelihood method”, and gives a flavour of the spirit in which we wrote the ASM book.

Best regards ---- Marc & Ken

messages.body_plain:
Dear Juliana,

this sounds like a fantastic data set and also a wonderful, because somewhat ‘excentric’, application of an occupancy model. Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).

About your two questions:
I would bet that the problem of individuals visiting multiple centers is so small that it can be ignored.
I am not sure about this and I would absolutely check out some spatial statistician’s opinion.

Couple other comments:
People are welcome to ask general questions about HMs such as occupancy models on this list, but obviously, as soon as it gets more specific about some software for which there are special, dedicated email lists, it might be better to ask there, or at least to also ask there. Jeff Doser now has an spOcc-Abu mailing list: https://groups.google.com/g/spocc-spabund-users. Jeff is unbelievably helpful and very knowledgeable about all sorts of spatial analyses, so I’d absolutely ask there as well
To me, the most important modeling rule is “Start simple”. While SVC models may in many ways be wonderful, they are also quite complex and may be hard to fit in practice. I’d suggest a progressive model building strategy, where you first investigate what nonspatial models can explain, then add in a simple spatial random field, and only then go to the full SVC model
What about false positives ? Are they rare enough that it is meaningful to ignore them ? Hopefully, since if not, then your life becomes much more challenging (and you wouldn’t be able to work with spOccupancy right now).
About 10 years ago some people worked specifically with disease applications of occupancy models, especially Brett McClintock, David Miller and some of their colleagues. Be sure to check out  this paper <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01472.x>, among others.

Good luck with your fascinating project !

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

It would be great to get some advice. I have camera trap data across 18 months which covers wet and dry seasons, spans across two years with some sites being sampled more than once while others just a single visit. Cameras were out in 3 month blocks but didn't always remain 'active' for the full time period so i was planning to use either 24hr replicates or 5 day block replicates.

I want to look at how species occupancy varies 1) spatially along the gradient of sites and with vegetation cover and 2) across seasons. Any advice on how best to unpick the spOccupancy options? I'm conscious of getting the correct interpretation between single- and multi- season models.

Really appreciate the advice in advance.
Felicity

messages.body_plain:
Hi Juliana--

This is a very interesting application.

The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I'd think of that more as an issue of spatial autocorrelation (nonindependence between hospitals covering overlapping precincts) rather than a violation of closure, so the spatial random effects you propose seem great to me. Aggregating nearby sites might make sense but I don't know whether it would resolve your spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, maybe there are demographic data associated with these facilities that you could use to investigate the spatial coverage of each?

I agree with Marc that the issue of the same infected individuals testing positive at multiple facilities sounds rare enough to be observed.

I think it will be very important to account for the variable "effort" between facilities with different testing rates. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). Curious to hear how others would handle this.

Best,
Ben

>

Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).

>

>

> I'm currently working on a data set containing reports of vector-borne diseases in Brazil (dengue, zika and chikungunya). I would like to use spOccupancy to fit multi-season spatially varying coefficient occupancy models to understand the occurrence of these diseases at a national level.

>
>
>

>
>

messages.body_plain:
I think the imperfect detection occurs when the disease is present at a site during a given week (or weeks), but the facility does not detect it on a given day.  Obviously this all depends on how the data are grouped to determine temporal periods of closure.

I do wonder if the Royle-Nichols occupancy formulation would make sense here, to account for the latent "abundance" of infected individuals influencing the probability of detection.

This bigger discussion has been great.  I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.

I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I'd think of that more as an issue of spatial autocorrelation (nonindependence between hospitals covering overlapping precincts) rather than a violation of closure, so the spatial random effects you propose seem great to me. Aggregating nearby sites might make sense but I don't know whether it would resolve your spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, maybe there are demographic data associated with these facilities that you could use to investigate the spatial coverage of each?
> >
> > I agree with Marc that the issue of the same infected individuals testing positive at multiple facilities sounds rare enough to be observed.
> >
> > I think it will be very important to account for the variable "effort" between facilities with different testing rates. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). messages.body_plain:
Hey,

So then perhaps the number of truly infected individuals z is binomially distributed where N is the number that came in and tested and psi is the infection prevalence

z ~ Binomial(N, psi)

where the number of positive tests y is binomially distributed with detection probability p

y ~ Binomial(z, p)

I'm not sure how well identified the detection and prevalence probabilities would be without some strong assumptions (such as the closure assumption we make in occupancy models).

> I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.

Agreed. More and more I'm just thinking of occupancy as accounting for zero-inflation, and I'm thinking less about the ecological interpretation of this zero-inflation.

Matt

On Wed, Nov 6, 2024 at 10:09 AM Daniel Linden <danl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I think the imperfect detection occurs when the disease is present at a site during a given week (or weeks), but the facility does not detect it on a given day.  Obviously this all depends on how the data are grouped to determine temporal periods of closure.
>
> I do wonder if the Royle-Nichols occupancy formulation would make sense here, to account for the latent "abundance" of infected individuals influencing the probability of detection.
>
> This bigger discussion has been great.  I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.
>
> On Tue, Nov 5, 2024 at 4:16 PM Matthijs Hollanders <matthijs....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Juliana and others,
> >
> > Forgive me for probably missing something simple, but what exactly is the imperfect detection component here?
> >
> > Matt
> >
> > On Wed, Nov 6, 2024 at 1:01 AM 'Benjamin R Goldstein' via hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Juliana--
> > >
> > > This is a very interesting application.
> > >
> > > The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I'd think of that more as an issue of spatial autocorrelation (nonindependence between hospitals covering overlapping precincts) rather than a violation of closure, so the spatial random effects you propose seem great to me. Aggregating nearby sites might make sense but I don't know whether it would resolve your spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, maybe there are demographic data associated with these facilities that you could use to investigate the spatial coverage of each?
> > >
> > > I agree with Marc that the issue of the same infected individuals testing positive at multiple facilities sounds rare enough to be observed.
> > >
> > > I think it will be very important to account for the variable "effort" between facilities with different testing rates. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). Curious to hear how others would handle this.
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Ben
> > >
> > > On Mon, Nov 4, 2024 at 11:06 AM Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Dear Juliana,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > this sounds like a fantastic data set and also a wonderful, because somewhat ‘excentric’, application of an occupancy model. Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > About your two questions:
> > > > I would bet that the problem of individuals visiting multiple centers is so small that it can be ignored.
> > > > I am not sure about this and I would absolutely check out some spatial statistician’s opinion.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Couple other comments:
> > > > People are welcome to ask general questions about HMs such as occupancy models on this list, but obviously, as soon as it gets more specific about some software for which there are special, dedicated email lists, it might be better to ask there, or at least to also ask there. Jeff Doser now has an spOcc-Abu mailing list: https://groups.google.com/g/spocc-spabund-users. Jeff is unbelievably helpful and very knowledgeable about all sorts of spatial analyses, so I’d absolutely ask there as well
> > > > To me, the most important modeling rule is “Start simple”. While SVC models may in many ways be wonderful, they are also quite complex and may be hard to fit in practice. I’d suggest a progressive model building strategy, where you first investigate what nonspatial models can explain, then add in a simple spatial random field, and only then go to the full SVC model
> > > > What about false positives ? Are they rare enough that it is meaningful to ignore them ? Hopefully, since if not, then your life becomes much more challenging (and you wouldn’t be able to work with spOccupancy right now).
> > > > About 10 years ago some people worked specifically with disease applications of occupancy models, especially Brett McClintock, David Miller and some of their colleagues. Be sure to check out  this paper <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01472.x>, among others.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Good luck with your fascinating project !
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Best regards  -- Marc

> > > > Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> Im Auftrag von Juliana Vélez

> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Hi all,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Marc's question about the definition of a site in camera-trap surveys motivated me to reach out for feedback about an analysis I'm conducting. It's an unusual use case for occupancy modeling, as far as I can tell.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I'm currently working on a data set containing reports of vector-borne diseases in Brazil (dengue, zika and chikungunya). I would like to use spOccupancy to fit multi-season spatially varying coefficient occupancy models to understand the occurrence of these diseases at a national level.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I have daily reports of disease occurrence, including negative test results, per health facility (i.e., 40K sites) for the last 5 years throughout Brazil. For my analysis, I plan to summarize these reports as weekly or biweekly detections. I'm very interested in using the occupancy framework, as these diseases are commonly underdetected and not diagnosed when present. These diseases are present for large periods of time (during summer and fall), so I plan to define seasons as semesters.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Before going forward with my analyses, I would love to hear your thoughts on two particular points:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > 1. Do you foresee any problem with applying occupancy models to the previously described disease data? Similar to camera traps, people with the disease can go to multiple sites (i.e., attend different health facilities), so the closure assumption might not be reasonable. Marc's email made me think more about the definition of my sites and the need to interpret the occupancy estimates as occurrence.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > 2. The distribution of the sites (i.e., health facilities) is not uniform. Some health facilities are very close to one another, especially in highly populated areas. If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thanks in advance for any thoughts/recommendations!
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Best regards,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Juliana

> > > > On Fri, Nov 1, 2024 at 12:27 PM 'John Clare' via hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Hey Marc and all,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Cheers,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > John

> > > > > From: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>

> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Dear all,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the  recent paper by Goldstein <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14359__;!!Mak6IKo!NX60gBNM93SYmtD8VFgF8ZKITUypQvav83s367dFdyMCCei4DMtHJd5jRIxpf4jgK1znDG6YPKRgyZVRtOJ89-3g$> et al.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Thank you for your thoughts on my questions! This discussion has been very helpful.

1. Imperfect detection: As Marc and Dan pointed out, imperfect detection is linked to the “testing gap” that arises because some proportion of the infected individuals within the area served by a health facility go untested (e.g., due to an inability to travel to the health facility or mild symptoms managed at home). The diseases I’m studying are largely underreported.

2. Spatial autocorrelation: Thanks, Marc and Ben, for your suggestions! I’ll check with Jeff Doser about how to handle nearby sites.

3. Variable “effort”: I like your idea of using the number of tests as a covariate, Ben. I had been thinking about including population in the area served by a health facility both in the detection model (more likely to detect the infection in larger populations) and in the occupancy model (the disease is more likely to be present in more populated areas). Dan, do you think that would address the issues that motivated the Royle-Nichols occupancy formulation, or is a more complex treatment necessary here? I have also been thinking about how population interacts with the density of health facilities to drive variation in per capita health care access/delivery (e.g., more potential patients per health facility in poor rural areas than in affluent urban areas).

Thanks again for sharing your perspectives!

Best regards,

Juliana

> Hey,
>
> So then perhaps the number of truly infected individuals z is binomially distributed where N is the number that came in and tested and psi is the infection prevalence
>
> z ~ Binomial(N, psi)
>
> where the number of positive tests y is binomially distributed with detection probability p
>
> y ~ Binomial(z, p)
>
> I'm not sure how well identified the detection and prevalence probabilities would be without some strong assumptions (such as the closure assumption we make in occupancy models).
>
> > I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.
>
> Agreed. More and more I'm just thinking of occupancy as accounting for zero-inflation, and I'm thinking less about the ecological interpretation of this zero-inflation.
>
> Matt
>
>
>
> On Wed, Nov 6, 2024 at 10:09 AM Daniel Linden <danl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I think the imperfect detection occurs when the disease is present at a site during a given week (or weeks), but the facility does not detect it on a given day.  Obviously this all depends on how the data are grouped to determine temporal periods of closure.
> >
> > I do wonder if the Royle-Nichols occupancy formulation would make sense here, to account for the latent "abundance" of infected individuals influencing the probability of detection.
> >
> > This bigger discussion has been great.  I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.

> > > > Hi Juliana--
> > > >
> > > > This is a very interesting application.
> > > >
> > > > The definition of a "site" in the sense of defining the unit of closure will be whatever geographic area a facility draws patients from. I guess more precisely it would be the set of people who might potentially get tested at a facility. It sounds like there will be some overlap between sites. I'd think of that more as an issue of spatial autocorrelation (nonindependence between hospitals covering overlapping precincts) rather than a violation of closure, so the spatial random effects you propose seem great to me. Aggregating nearby sites might make sense but I don't know whether it would resolve your spatial autocorrelation. Additionally, maybe there are demographic data associated with these facilities that you could use to investigate the spatial coverage of each?
> > > >
> > > > I agree with Marc that the issue of the same infected individuals testing positive at multiple facilities sounds rare enough to be observed.
> > > >
> > > > I think it will be very important to account for the variable "effort" between facilities with different testing rates. I guess that could be represented by the total number of tests, positive + negative, at each site, which could be associated with both detection (more likely to detect an infection in a population if each individual is more likely to test) as well as occupancy (the disease is more likely to be present in 1 person if the population served is larger). > > > > > Dear Juliana,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > this sounds like a fantastic data set and also a wonderful, because somewhat ‘excentric’, application of an occupancy model. Basically, I think that an occupancy model is very much applicable to spatiotemporal modeling of these diseases, because it can take account of one of the typical measurement errors present in such reports, false negatives. I believe that the false-negative probability will refer both to the case where a person who has a disease fails to be diagnosed when visiting a center, and also to the case where a disease is present in the catchment area of a health facility (or whatever else you end up defining as a site) but none of the people who visit a center have it (though I am not totally sure…).
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > About your two questions:
> > > > > I would bet that the problem of individuals visiting multiple centers is so small that it can be ignored.
> > > > > I am not sure about this and I would absolutely check out some spatial statistician’s opinion.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Couple other comments:

Jeff is unbelievably helpful and very knowledgeable about all sorts of spatial analyses, so I’d absolutely ask there as well

I’d suggest a progressive model building strategy, where you first investigate what nonspatial models can explain, then add in a simple spatial random field, and only then go to the full SVC model
> > > > > What about false positives ? Are they rare enough that it is meaningful to ignore them ? Hopefully, since if not, then your life becomes much more challenging (and you wouldn’t be able to work with spOccupancy right now).
> > > > > About 10 years ago some people worked specifically with disease applications of occupancy models, especially Brett McClintock, David Miller and some of their colleagues. Be sure to check out  this paper <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01472.x>, among others.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Good luck with your fascinating project !
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Best regards  -- Marc

> > > > > Marc's question about the definition of a site in camera-trap surveys motivated me to reach out for feedback about an analysis I'm conducting. It's an unusual use case for occupancy modeling, as far as I can tell.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm currently working on a data set containing reports of vector-borne diseases in Brazil (dengue, zika and chikungunya). I would like to use spOccupancy to fit multi-season spatially varying coefficient occupancy models to understand the occurrence of these diseases at a national level.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I have daily reports of disease occurrence, including negative test results, per health facility (i.e., 40K sites) for the last 5 years throughout Brazil. For my analysis, I plan to summarize these reports as weekly or biweekly detections. I'm very interested in using the occupancy framework, as these diseases are commonly underdetected and not diagnosed when present. These diseases are present for large periods of time (during summer and fall), so I plan to define seasons as semesters.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Before going forward with my analyses, I would love to hear your thoughts on two particular points:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 1. Do you foresee any problem with applying occupancy models to the previously described disease data? Similar to camera traps, people with the disease can go to multiple sites (i.e., attend different health facilities), so the closure assumption might not be reasonable. > > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 2. The distribution of the sites (i.e., health facilities) is not uniform. Some health facilities are very close to one another, especially in highly populated areas. If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?

> > > > > > I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

> > > > > >
> > > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best regards  --- Marc

Ecological networks are often inferred from field data to understand interactions between organisms at different trophic levels. Typically, this involves capturing the interacting organism (e.g., a seed disperser, pollinator, or host of a parasite/pathogen) and/or detecting evidence of the interaction (e.g., feces, blood, or even the parasite itself). Naturally, this process is imperfect and involves multiple sources of uncertainty.

For instance, consider a mutualistic plant-bird interaction where evidence of seed dispersal of plant X by bird Y is gathered from fecal samples collected along an elevational gradient. At the ecological level, several uncertainties are present: Bird Y may or may not occupy a given site, plant X may or may not occupy a given site, and, even if both are present at the same site, their interaction may or may not occur at that site.

Moreover, assuming the interaction does occur, additional sampling uncertainties arise: the bird may or may not be captured, a fecal sample may or may not be collected from it, and even if a sample is collected, it may or may not contain a seed of plant X.

These uncertainties seem well-suited for modeling with an hierarchical occupancy framework, especially within a multispecies, multi-interaction model. Temporal replication could provide insights into the probability of detecting bird Y given its presence, while fecal samples from multiple dispersers at a site could help infer the presence of plant X. However, I also wonder if these cumulative uncertainties would not require a prohibitively large dataset to estimate parameters with acceptable precision.

With this in mind, I briefly searched for such a model in the literature but could not find anything. Thus, I would like to know if anyone has already tested and published a model of this type or if this is still a work to be done.

messages.subject: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

My name is Luca Petroni. I am currently working on interspecific spatial interactions among carnivores, but I am encountering fit issues in occupancy models using a "stacked" dataset.

Specifically, my dataset consists of continuous camera-trapping data collected over a year across 50 sites in a mountainous region. I stacked the data by month, resulting in 600 site-months (50 sites × 12 months) with 10 survey occasions (detection/non-detections aggregated by 3 days). I have been fitting the models in JAGS using jagsUI, incorporating a random site effect on species occupancy to account for pseudo-replication, and adding covariates for both occupancy and detection probabilities. Additionally, I used the goodness-of-fit assessment code from AHM2, summarizing the detections by site-month (row). Unfortunately, my results show a severe lack of fit for all the models, regardless of the combinations of covariates used, with Bayesian p-values of 0.

Interestingly, the fit only improves when introducing random site-month effects (i.e., 600 random terms per species) on detection probabilities. Therefore, I tested the fit of single-species models too (in spOccupancy), and the results were the same for all of them: bpv= 0. In this case, however, adding a random site effect on the detection probability was enough to obtain decent fit for most species. However, for the widespread and more abundant ones, only adding the random site-month effect worked out the fit issues.
Referring to MacKenzie and Bailey’s 2004 paper, this severe lack of fit may stem from a higher-than-expected frequency of detection histories with all 1s, which are indeed present for those abundant and widespread species in our study. Since I tested various covariates, unexplained site heterogeneity seems an unlikely cause. Instead, local differences in species density may be a more plausible explanation, particularly for widespread species, also given the stacked structure of my dataset, which includes repeated monthly sampling at the same sites. I even tried to fit the models on daily detection/non-detection data (i.e., 30 survey occasions), to increase the potential variability in the detection histories, but the results were always the same.

I would greatly appreciate your perspective on this issue. Do you think adding a random site-month effect on detection probabilities is justified in this context? Or might there be alternative strategies you’d recommend to address this lack of fit, especially given the size and structure of our dataset?
Thank you all in advance for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Luca Petroni

messages.body_plain:
Hey Luca,

In my experience, having bad BPVs with these types of models is quite common unless you essentially overfit with adding those random effects. Are you assessing the BPV for each species, or all of them together?

Also, I'm pretty sure we've collectively been doing this PPCs "wrong" with these models. It is typical to condition the posterior predictive distribution on your latent occupancy states, i.e., yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(z[i] * p[i, j]), where i and j reference sites and surveys, respectively. However, this isn't really the posterior predictive distribution. For that, you should do zrep[i] ~ dbern(psi[i]), yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(zrep[i] * p[i, j]), i.e., first simulating new z's and then simulating yreps conditional on them. I don't think it'll make your lack of fit go away, but you could give it a crack. Some of the posterior predictive plotting functionality in the bayesplot is quite useful for visualising the posterior predictive predictive distribution alongside your observed data. I assume your model includes species random effects, btw?

Cheers,

Matt

Dear Matt,

thanks for the answer. I usually calculate the chi-squared discrepancy separately for all the species but sum them to have a measure of the overall model fit.

I was also thinking about simulating new presence/absence as you suggested, but I tried going single-species with the spOccupancy functions before adding to the JAGS models. Nevertheless, the single-species models fitted in spOccupancy highlighted the same issue, but I did not verify how the discrepancy measures are computed in the ppcOcc( ) function.

As for your last point, the multi-species model includes a random site effect on single-species natural parameters (I have 4 target species, so f1, f2, f3 and f4) but none on the co-occurrence natural parameters (f12, f13, f14, f23, f24, f34, as I only considered pairwise interactions). Then, I have another random site effect on  the detection probabilities for all the species (p1, p2, p3 and p4), but for at least two of them the site-month random is needed, otherwise the overall fit goes to 0.

I do not have random species effects. Should I include them? What is the rationale behind this choice?

Thanks again.

Best,
Luca

messages.body_plain:
Dear Matt,

the model is basically mirroring the multi-species model with interactions from Rota et al. (2016), the same that is implemented in the unmakred package through the occuMulti( ) function. It accounts for interactions among species, therefore their occupancy probabilities are linked and not estimated independently. Specifically, Z is defined as a categorical with x possible values,with x=16 for 4 species: 0000,1000, 0100, 0010, 0001, 1100, 1010, and so on (a multivariate binomial) each with its own probability Psi[x], and natural parameters for single-species occupancy and co-occurrence are expressed as log[Psi[x]/(1-Psi[x])].
I have never found random species effects used in this modelling framework, but i could try and see where it will get me.

Moreover, I can tell you another interesting thing supporting my guess about differences in local densities. Adding a simple measure of detection rate (number of detections in a month divided by days the camera was active in the month) as a covariate on detection probability in single-species models always drags the bpv to exactly 1. However, there is no way I can control for such punctual/local differences, especially in a stacked framework.

Best,

Luca

Hey Luca,

Nevermind, I wasn't familiar with the model structure. I thought you were just estimating psi and wanted to make sure you were doing so separately for each species.

Have you considered a different observation model? You could use the observed counts of detections with a Poisson observation model instead of a binary observation model where you essentially collapse those counts to 1s and 0s. I'm not sure to what extent that will help with your model fit, but it should help you hone in on your detection rates a bit better.

Cheers,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hey,

There's a few things you could do. You could just model the number of detections per species and day (or whatever occasion interval you choose) as Poisson distribution, i.e., y[i, j, m] ~ dpois(lambda[i, j, m]), where you model the site-, survey-, and species-specific detection rates lambda. However, this ignores the non-independence of detections, i.e. with the same animal moving past the device multiple times. Clark Rushing wrote a paper <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2656.13902> about continuous time CMR where you can account for that with a Hawkes process, which is a self-exciting process that essentially lets prior observations influence the detection rates of next observations (i.e., detection peaks right after an individual is detected becasue it might trigger the camera more than once or it might be a few animals together). For this you have to specify the log-likelihood which I know how to do in Stan, but not in JAGS, but I'm sure someone can help you. I think you need the zeros or ones trick which I never wrapped my head around.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

many thanks for your many, valuable and thought-provoking messages about my question. Makes me think that perhaps the most neglected part of all the quantitative things we do is study design and that perhaps a book ought to be written about sampling design in species distribution models.

Best regards  --- Marc

From: John Clare <jcl...@wisc.edu>
Sent: Friday, November 1, 2024 18:27
To: Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>; hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?

Hey Marc and all,

I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made.

You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.

Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.

In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.

Cheers,

John

From: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Marc Kery <marc...@vogelwarte.ch>
Sent: Thursday, October 31, 2024 2:08 PM
To: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?

Dear all,

I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.

The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.

Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the  recent paper by Goldstein <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14359__;!!Mak6IKo!NX60gBNM93SYmtD8VFgF8ZKITUypQvav83s367dFdyMCCei4DMtHJd5jRIxpf4jgK1znDG6YPKRgyZVRtOJ89-3g$> et al.

My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).

On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.

Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hi Marc and all,

Sorry for being late to the discussion, but just caught up to it.

I actually used occupancy models for a similar camera-trap data set. We had information on 8 species, which we analyzed as single-species, dynamic occupancy models.
It was 11 years of data, 121 camera-trap sites, imbalanced data between different species too.
Cameras were active year-round for 24/7, motion triggered. There were also missing data years, which we treated as NA.
The focus of our analysis was seasonality, so we pooled data into months, and my primary occasions were seasons, and secondary occasions were months within seasons for repetition to calculate detection too.
Cameras were roughly in the center of 2 x 2 km2 grids, therefore, as Marc wrote in his previous e-mail, we calculated more like a "probability of use".
Since we were interested in changes in the habitat use with seasons, our focus was more on colonization and local extinction (which we called "desertion" for the same reason with "probability of use).
This work is published: https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/article/105/1/122/7450311
Code is also on GitHub: https://github.com/dilsaddt/NorthAnatolia_2022_singlesp_seasonal_habitat_use

If this could be helpful to anyone, I'm glad.
And of course if there are any questions I'm happy to answer.
Best,
Dilsad

Hi Juliana,

just reading up some on false positive models and the  Guillera-Arroita et al. (MEE, 2017) <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/2041-210X.12743> paper made me think that perhaps you might consider multi-level occupancy models. Perhaps that might be another way to dealing with spatial structure in the occurrence of the disease ? In addition, you may want to think about false positives in addition to false negatives. Standard occupancy models deal with the latter, but to deal with the former you normally need some additional information.

See also the paper by  John Clare and colleagues <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ecy.3241>, which extends consideration from simple occupancy to abundance and other population metrics.

Best regards  --- Marc

Hey,

So then perhaps the number of truly infected individuals z is binomially distributed where N is the number that came in and tested and psi is the infection prevalence

z ~ Binomial(N, psi)

where the number of positive tests y is binomially distributed with detection probability p

y ~ Binomial(z, p)

> I think the issue of occupancy in continuous habitat is still confusing and poorly understood, despite all the literature the past few years.

Hi Marc,

Thanks for giving more thought to my question!

The dataset I'm working with has information on diagnostic criteria, including laboratory-based detection methods. These detections are based on NS1 antigens (with reported false positive rates in the literature ranging from 0.5% to 10%), IgM antibodies (false positive rates of 8–10%), and RT-PCR (false positive rates of 2–5%). I agree it'd be worth exploring the approaches proposed by Guillera-Arroita et al. and Clare et al.

Thanks again for the additional recommendations!

Juliana

> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I have daily reports of disease occurrence, including negative test results, per health facility (i.e., 40K sites) for the last 5 years throughout Brazil. For my analysis, I plan to summarize these reports as weekly or biweekly detections. I'm very interested in using the occupancy framework, as these diseases are commonly underdetected and not diagnosed when present. These diseases are present for large periods of time (during summer and fall), so I plan to define seasons as semesters.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Before going forward with my analyses, I would love to hear your thoughts on two particular points:
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 1. Do you foresee any problem with applying occupancy models to the previously described disease data? Similar to camera traps, people with the disease can go to multiple sites (i.e., attend different health facilities), so the closure assumption might not be reasonable. Marc's email made me think more about the definition of my sites and the need to interpret the occupancy estimates as occurrence.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 2. The distribution of the sites (i.e., health facilities) is not uniform. Some health facilities are very close to one another, especially in highly populated areas. If I'm extracting covariates for example within a 10 km buffer, some of this information will overlap for close health facilities. I'm thinking about using spatial random effects to account for spatial autocorrelation. Would this be sufficient to deal with this problem, or would you recommend grouping health facilities that are within some distance of each other?
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks in advance for any thoughts/recommendations!
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Best regards,
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Juliana
> > > > >

> > > > >
> > > > > On Fri, Nov 1, 2024 at 12:27 PM 'John Clare' via hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hey Marc and all,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I think it depends on what you want to achieve. If focusing on describing psi/z at the specific camera locations or trying to estimate a PAO in the Efford 2012 sense, I agree that there's no decision about site size that needs to be made.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > You do need (or it makes things easier, at least) a site size for predicting/mapping. There's lots of literature (Hayes and Monfils 2015 JWM, Eric Nielson et al. 2019 Ecosphere, and papers that Ben linked to) that focus on scale and bias and whether a point detector can describe occupancy in some broader patch. Mileage may vary. I'm not entirely convinced there is a general rule for spacing/scale with respect to bias (etc.) and my sense is that many of the demonstrated issues more generally arise from unexplained (or unmodeled) detection heterogeineity and lack of fit.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Maybe the way I'd approach this from the perspective that "size" is  an explicit design consideration that is linked to the sample selection procedure. E.g., if the sampling frame is just one big continuous space and you use an rng to generate a sample of points in that space, then the site is essentially the camera location or some very small unit. If the sampling frame is a collection of cells and the sampling selection process randomly picks some cells (in which cameras are then placed), the site is the size of a cell. Making one  design decision or another largely depends on interest in coarser or finer aspects of animal space use, pragmatic things like predictor resolution, etc.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In the case here where the design is imposed after the fact, I think I'd primarily worry about the design being non-ignorable if I were mapping or tying to make some broader inference about a set of sites. Maybe the way I'd approach this is to get a sense of where cameras could have been placed and then try to reverse engineer a sampling frame consisting of sites with relatively equitable inclusion probability. E.g., if all the cameras are on dirt roads and I wanted to explore space use at some really fine grain (say, 10 m), I'd probably mask out off-road "sites" that had no probability of being selected. If there was no possibility of sampling above some elevation, I'd either mask out higher mountain peaks, or make the cells large enough such that it was potentially plausible that any site might have contained a camera.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Cheers,

> > > > > > I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the  recent paper by Goldstein <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14359__;!!Mak6IKo!NX60gBNM93SYmtD8VFgF8ZKITUypQvav83s367dFdyMCCei4DMtHJd5jRIxpf4jgK1znDG6YPKRgyZVRtOJ89-3g$> et al.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.
